Financial planning · Inflation-linked bond cash flows · Visual planning guide

An inflation-linked bond has three different amounts: adjusted principal, coupon cash and redemption

Use four interactive USD charts to separate an index adjustment from spendable coupon cash, apply a maturity principal floor and compare redemption with an independently entered purchase outlay.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 25 October 2026 · 5 min read
Sources reviewed 25 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Separate index-adjusted principal from the cash a bond actually pays

Interactive planning lab

Coupon cash received before the maturity date · USD$969.73
Principal cash repaid at maturity · USD$11,592.74
Maturity principal minus purchase outlay · USD$1,092.74

Original USD illustration of an inflation-indexed bond, not an actual TIPS quote, observed CPI series or investment recommendation. The reference price index starts at 1 and compounds at the selected constant annual rate; half-year index levels use fractional powers. Coupons are paid at each half-year end on the then-adjusted principal. Principal may fall below original face before maturity; the original-face floor is applied only to principal redemption, never to the coupon calculation. This simplified schedule omits actual TIPS daily reference-CPI conventions, publication lag, interpolation, accrued interest and settlement rounding. The purchase outlay is entered independently as a percentage of original face; no market yield or fair price is estimated. All coupons are retained as cash earning zero interest and are never added to indexed principal. No fees, tax, default, early sale, fund distributions or currency conversion is included. Base-year coupon amounts divide each payment by the same model index at its own payment date; they are not the purchasing power of an accumulated cash account at maturity. USD indexation does not establish protection for a CAD spending goal or a personal spending basket.

The central idea

Match a spending date with an actual cash payment. Index-adjusted principal, market value and purchase outlay are different amounts, and a floor on original face does not promise every purchase price back.

01

Start with the cash-flow question, then identify the amount

A retirement budget may need money this month, while a bond’s principal is scheduled to be repaid years later. An increase in an indexed principal amount does not itself fill that month’s spending account. The useful first question is when cash is actually paid.

TreasuryDirect’s TIPS overview describes U.S. Treasury Inflation-Protected Securities: principal adjusts with inflation or deflation, the coupon rate is fixed, and interest is paid every six months on adjusted principal. At maturity, principal redemption is the greater of the adjusted amount and original principal.

The charts use those basic distinctions in an authored USD example. They do not reproduce a security’s daily index ratios or a market quotation. Keep four labels separate: original face, index-adjusted principal, coupon receipts and the amount actually paid to buy the bond. A secondary-market sale value would be another amount requiring its own calculation.

02

Specify the reference index and the payment convention

The default begins with USD 10,000 of original face and a reference index of 1. Its illustrative index rises at a constant 3% annually over five years. Half-year checkpoints use fractional compounding, so the index at time t is 1.03 raised to the power t.

At year five, adjusted principal is approximately USD 11,592.74. The increase above USD 10,000 remains part of the principal calculation; it has not also been paid as five separate annual cash bonuses. The first chart therefore shows principal amounts rather than a bank-account balance.

For an actual TIPS, TreasuryDirect provides security-specific daily index ratios. A real calculation requires the matching security and payment date. This model substitutes a smooth authored index and omits reference-CPI publication lag, daily interpolation and settlement rounding. Its index is neither observed U.S. inflation nor a forecast.

03

Multiply the fixed coupon rate by the changing principal base

The selected annual coupon rate is 2%. A half-year payment is adjusted principal on that payment date multiplied by 1%. It is not 1% of the purchase price, and a principal index increase is not another coupon.

TreasuryDirect’s pricing explanation uses original principal times the applicable index ratio, then half the stated annual coupon rate, to calculate a TIPS payment. The chart’s simpler index follows that multiplication structure without claiming to reproduce an actual payment.

The grouped bars total the two nominal coupons received in each model year. Beside them, each coupon is divided by the illustrative index at its own payment date before the two reference-date amounts are added. That comparison remains USD 200 per year. It describes the purchasing power of the payment flows under the same index, rather than the later value of accumulated cash.

04

Apply the original-face floor at redemption, not at every checkpoint

Change the annual index movement to a negative figure. Adjusted principal declines, and so do nominal coupon payments. The dashed original-face reference does not stop that interim decline. In this illustration, the final coupon is still calculated from adjusted principal even when it is below face.

At maturity, the separate principal payment is the larger of adjusted principal and original face. Under five years of constant 4% annual deflation, for example, adjusted principal is about USD 8,153.73, while the modeled principal redemption is USD 10,000. The floor supplies the difference at that date.

That maturity calculation is not a quote for selling the bond earlier. Nor does it guarantee that an amount paid above original face will be returned as principal. The matrix compares redemption with several authored purchase outlays and excludes coupons explicitly. A negative cell identifies a principal-only difference; it does not establish the full investment loss.

05

Count coupons and redemption once, then subtract the purchase outlay

The default purchase outlay is 105% of original face, or USD 10,500. This amount is entered independently. The model does not solve for a market yield, assess whether that price is attractive or imply that coupon rate equals return.

The waterfall adds all received coupons and the maturity principal payment, then subtracts the purchase outlay. It assumes every coupon is retained as cash earning zero interest. The maturity payment already contains the applicable index adjustment or original-face floor, so adding a separate inflation uplift would count part of principal twice.

The resulting nominal cash difference is not an annualized or inflation-adjusted return. Coupons arrive at different dates, and cash held without interest can lose purchasing power during inflation. Spending those coupons would reduce the cash still available at maturity. Reinvesting them would require a separate rate and timing assumption; neither action is silently included here.

06

Match the currency, price index and payment date to the actual need

To use this distinction in a financial plan, list the dates and currency of the required payments. Place expected coupon receipts beside those dates, and reserve the principal payment for maturity. A bill due earlier needs another identified source of cash or an explicit sale assumption.

These USD charts do not demonstrate protection for a Canadian-dollar bill. Currency conversion changes the CAD amount received, while a household’s spending basket can move differently from a broad consumer price index. Taxes and transaction costs can also separate gross contractual payments from spendable household cash; neither is calculated here.

The related bond-horizon article examines sale values and reinvestment separately, and the currency guide explains translation into CAD. This page stops at contractual cash-flow arithmetic under its selected index. It supplies no actual bond price path, fund return, tax estimate or personal allocation target. Use a real security’s terms and dated index ratios before treating a chart as a payment forecast.

Sources and scope

Public sources reviewed on 25 October 2026. All four charts are original hypothetical USD calculations. TreasuryDirect sources explain real TIPS mechanics; no actual security, CPI observation, yield quote, tax result or CAD hedge is modeled. Original scenario calculations and research checklists are TickerLantern’s educational analysis; attributed publisher examples retain their stated source and scope. Recheck current issuer documents for any product-specific decision.

  1. TreasuryDirect · Treasury Inflation-Protected Securities (TIPS) ↗

    Reviewed 25 October 2026. Primary source for variable indexed principal, fixed coupon rate, semiannual interest and the original-principal maturity floor. The floor concerns original principal; the authored purchase outlay is separately defined.

  2. TreasuryDirect · Understanding pricing and interest rates ↗

    Reviewed 25 October 2026. The TIPS section explains multiplying original principal by the matching index ratio and then by half the stated annual coupon rate. No current yield or auction price is copied into this model.

  3. TreasuryDirect · TIPS/CPI indexes ↗

    Reviewed 25 October 2026. Actual calculations use security-specific index ratios for matching payment dates. This article uses an invented smooth index instead of official observations and does not reproduce the daily reference-CPI calculation.
